cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What does Roman property law deal with?
cards.back:
With the attribution of legal objects (things, RES) to legal subjects — ie with property rights.
• Things are the objects of legal transactions; the legal subject can use them and dispose of them.
• Cf § 285 ABGB: a thing is “everything that differs from and is subject to use by humans”.
cards.old_front: Womit befasst sich das römische Sachenrecht?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What is a legal subject? What does legal personality mean?
cards.back:
Legal subject = anyone who can be the bearer of rights and duties (a person in the legal sense).
• Legal personality = the capacity to have rights and duties.
• For the freeborn it begins at birth (born alive and of human form).
cards.old_front: Was ist ein Rechtssubjekt (legal subject)? Was bedeutet Rechtsfähigkeit (legal personality)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What did a person's legal status depend on in Rome (unlike today)?
cards.back:
On an interplay of several factors — today all human beings have equal legal personality (§ 16 ABGB, § 1 BGB, Art 11 ZGB).
• Liberty (STATUS LIBERTATIS)
• Citizenship (STATUS CIVITATIS)
• Position in the family (STATUS FAMILIAE)
• Gender
cards.old_front: Wovon hing die Rechtsstellung einer Person in Rom ab (anders als heute)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: STATUS LIBERTATIS: how does Roman law distinguish free persons and slaves?
cards.back:
HOMINES LIBERI (free persons) vs SERVI (slaves); free persons are INGENUI (freeborn) or LIBERTI (freedmen).
• Slaves have no legal personality and are regarded as things — they can be sold or pledged.
• Under certain circumstances, however, they can acquire rights or incur obligations for their DOMINUS.
cards.old_front: STATUS LIBERTATIS: Wie unterscheidet das römische Recht Freie und Sklaven?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What does the principle NASCITURUS PRO IAM NATO HABETUR … state?
cards.back:
The unborn child is treated as already born insofar as its advantage is concerned (… QUOTIENS DE COMMODIS EIUS AGITUR).
• In itself, the NASCITURUS has no legal personality.
• Consequence: a child born after the father's death can inherit.
• Source: Paulus D 1.5.7; cf § 22 ABGB.
cards.old_front: Was besagt der Grundsatz NASCITURUS PRO IAM NATO HABETUR …?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: STATUS FAMILIAE: who is in the PATRIA POTESTAS of the PATER FAMILIAS?
cards.back:
The children of the house (FILII/FILIAE FAMILIAS): all legitimate children, the legitimate descendants of sons still in power, and adopted children; in a MANUS marriage also the wife (UXOR IN MANU).
• Even adult children remain in power, unless by emancipation or transfer to another family (eg marriage).
• From the imperial period onwards, marriage without MANUS is the rule.
cards.old_front: STATUS FAMILIAE: Wer steht in der PATRIA POTESTAS des PATER FAMILIAS?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Are persons in power (children of the house, UXOR IN MANU) unfree? Can they hold property?
cards.back:
They are free (they have STATUS LIBERTATIS), but cannot hold property of their own.
• As long as they are in PATRIA POTESTAS, they are incapable of holding property.
• They can, however, acquire possession, ownership and other positions FOR their PATER FAMILIAS.
cards.old_front: Sind Gewaltunterworfene (Hauskinder, UXOR IN MANU) unfrei? Können sie Vermögen haben?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: STATUS CIVITATIS: which rights were reserved to Roman citizens?
cards.back:
Besides political rights, eg civil (Quiritary) ownership — DOMINIUM EX IURE QUIRITIUM — and certain transactions such as MANCIPATIO.
• Non-Romans could be granted COMMERCIUM → equal standing in legal transactions.
cards.old_front: STATUS CIVITATIS: Welche Rechte waren römischen Bürgern vorbehalten?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Does Roman law recognise legal persons? Give examples.
cards.back:
Yes — certain groups of persons and pools of assets count as independent bearers of rights.
• UNIVERSITATES (corporations), COLLEGIA, SODALITATES (associations); RES PUBLICA, MUNICIPIA, COLONIAE; professional and religious associations, burial societies, PIAE CAUSAE, SOCIETATES PUBLICANORUM.
• They can hold rights (eg ownership) and conclude transactions through representatives; rights and duties do not affect the members.
cards.old_front: Kennt das römische Recht juristische Personen? Nenne Beispiele.

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What does Ulpian D 3.4.7.1 say about corporations?
cards.back:
What is owed to the corporation is not owed to the individual members — and what it owes, the members do not owe.
• SI QUID UNIVERSITATI DEBETUR, SINGULIS NON DEBENTUR: NEC QUOD DEBET UNIVERSITAS DEBENT SINGULI.
• The corporation exists independently of its members.
cards.old_front: Was sagt Ulpian D 3.4.7.1 über Körperschaften?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Legal personality vs legal capacity — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Legal personality = being able to have rights and duties (from birth); legal capacity = being able to acquire rights and incur obligations through one's own acts.
• Legal capacity requires maturity in terms of age and mental state.
• Example Agerius: an orphan is a legal subject and heir from birth, but the inheritance is administered by a TUTOR.
cards.old_front: Rechtsfähigkeit vs Handlungsfähigkeit (legal capacity) — worin liegt der Unterschied?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Into which two parts is legal capacity divided?
cards.back:
1. Capacity to act: acquiring rights and incurring obligations through legal transactions, esp. contracts.
2. Criminal capacity: being responsible for unlawful conduct and liable for damages.
cards.old_front: In welche zwei Teile gliedert sich die Handlungsfähigkeit (legal capacity)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Which age thresholds are decisive for legal capacity in Roman law?
cards.back:
• INFANTES (post-classically up to 7 years): no legal capacity.
• IMPUBERES INFANTIA MAIORES / PUPILLI (boys 7–14, girls 7–12): limited capacity to act — only purely advantageous transactions; AUCTORITAS TUTORIS needed to incur obligations/dispose.
• PUBERTAS (girls at the end of their 12th, boys at the end of their 14th year): full capacity to act.
• MINORES (under 25): protection by the LEX (P)LAETORIA.
cards.old_front: Welche Altersstufen sind im römischen Recht für die Handlungsfähigkeit maßgeblich?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What can a PUPILLUS do without his tutor's consent?
cards.back:
Only transactions that bring him exclusively advantages (eg accepting a gift, release from a debt).
• To incur obligations or transfer rights (eg ownership), he needs the AUCTORITAS TUTORIS.
• I 1.21 pr: he can improve his position without a tutor, but not worsen it.
cards.old_front: Was kann ein PUPILLUS ohne Zustimmung seines Tutors tun?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What is a NEGOTIUM CLAUDICANS?
cards.back:
A “limping transaction”: a PUPILLUS concludes a contract with reciprocal obligations without AUCTORITAS TUTORIS.
• Only the part that confers rights on the PUPILLUS is valid; his own obligations do not become binding.
• Ulpian D 19.1.13.29: whoever buys from a PUPILLUS without his tutor is bound to him, but the PUPILLUS is not bound to the buyer.
• Today: the transaction is pending until the representative approves it (§ 151 ABGB, § 108 BGB, Art 19 ZGB).
cards.old_front: Was ist ein NEGOTIUM CLAUDICANS?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: To what extent was the PUPILLUS liable to the buyer under Ulpian D 19.1.13.29 if the tutor did not consent?
cards.back:
Contractually not at all — the contract binds only the buyer.
• Under a rescript of Antoninus Pius, however, the PUPILLUS can be sued for unjust enrichment (D 26.8.5 pr).
cards.old_front: Bis wann war der Pupill nach Ulpian D 19.1.13.29 gegenüber dem Käufer haftbar, wenn der Tutor nicht zustimmt?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Dispute between the schools: when did a boy come of age (PUBERTAS)?
cards.back:
Sabinians: individually — when he assumed the TOGA VIRILIS.
Proculians: a general age limit of 14 years.
• By Justinian's time at the latest, the Proculian view prevailed.
cards.old_front: Schulenstreit: Wann wurde ein Knabe mündig (PUBERTAS)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: How does Roman law protect MINORES (under 25)?
cards.back:
Through the LEX (P)LAETORIA (around 200 BC): deliberately exploiting a minor's inexperience is punishable.
• The praetor grants an EXCEPTIO LEGIS LAETORIAE or RESTITUTIO IN INTEGRUM — even for transactions that are merely objectively disadvantageous.
• In addition, a CURATOR MINORIS can advise; only at the end of the Diocletianic period does his consent become a requirement for validity.
cards.old_front: Wie schützt das römische Recht MINORES (unter 25)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Which restrictions applied to women; what is the TUTELA MULIERIS?
cards.back:
Women were excluded from public office and from power over a household; even a woman free of power (SUI IURIS) needed a TUTOR MULIERIS after PUBERTAS.
• Formal transactions (eg MANCIPATIO) and obligations only with his consent.
• In the high classical period merely a formality (Gai Inst 1.190: the tutor can be compelled by the praetor to consent).
cards.old_front: Welche Beschränkungen trafen Frauen; was ist die TUTELA MULIERIS?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: How are FURIOSI and PRODIGI treated in Roman law?
cards.back:
FURIOSUS (mentally disabled person): no legal capacity and no criminal capacity; a CURATOR FURIOSI is appointed for him.
PRODIGUS (spendthrift who endangers the maintenance of his family): can be declared incapable by the praetor (INTERDICTIO); he then acts himself only where purely advantageous, otherwise through a curator.
cards.old_front: Wie werden FURIOSI und PRODIGI im römischen Recht behandelt?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Which two features characterise property rights (rights in rem)?
cards.back:
1. They relate to a specific thing and entitle the holder to access and use it in a certain way.
2. They are absolute — to be respected by all members of the legal community.
• Expressed in Rome by ACTIONES IN REM (enforceable against everyone).
cards.old_front: Welche zwei Merkmale kennzeichnen dingliche Rechte (rights in rem)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Absolute vs relative rights — how are they enforced in Rome?
cards.back:
Absolute (property) rights are effective against everyone → ACTIO IN REM.
Relative rights (eg the buyer's claim to delivery) exist only between creditor and debtor → ACTIO IN PERSONAM.
cards.old_front: Absolute vs relative Rechte — wie werden sie in Rom durchgesetzt?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Example 1 (Clara, vase): Clara gives the vase to the banker Midas for safekeeping; the thief Hector steals it and sells/delivers it to Ago, who passes it on to Leander. Clara discovers it at Leander's. What can she do?
cards.back:
Clara can bring an ACTIO IN REM (REI VINDICATIO) against Leander, because she has a property right in the vase.
• Property rights are enforceable against any possessor.
cards.old_front: Beispiel 1 (Clara, Vase): Clara gibt die Vase dem Bankier Midas zur Verwahrung; Dieb Hector stiehlt sie und verkauft/übergibt sie an Ago, dieser an Leander. Clara entdeckt sie bei Leander. Was kann sie tun?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Why does Roman law recognise property rights only in corporeal things (RES CORPORALES)?
cards.back:
Because for the Romans control over an object is conceivable only for things that can be touched — QUI TANGI POSSUNT.
• Examples: land, a table, a ring, in Rome also a slave.
• Rights are incorporeal → in principle no property right in a right (exception: PIGNUS NOMINIS).
• The ABGB defines things more broadly (§ 285; § 292 “which fall within the senses”).
cards.old_front: Warum kennt das römische Recht nur Sachenrechte an körperlichen Sachen (RES CORPORALES)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Which property rights does Roman law recognise, and by which ACTIO IN REM is each protected?
cards.back:
• Ownership (DOMINIUM, PROPRIETAS) → REI VINDICATIO
• Servitudes (SERVITUTES) → VINDICATIO SERVITUTIS
• Right of pledge (PIGNUS) → VINDICATIO PIGNORIS (= ACTIO PIGNERATICIA IN REM)
• Hereditary lease (EMPHYTEUSIS) → REI VINDICATIO UTILIS
• Hereditary building right (SUPERFICIES) → ACTIO DE SUPERFICIE
cards.old_front: Welche dinglichen Rechte kennt das römische Recht und mit welcher ACTIO IN REM werden sie geschützt?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What does “numerus clausus of property rights” mean?
cards.back: The number of property rights is limited: no new types can be created by private legal transactions.
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet „numerus clausus der Sachenrechte“?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: Example Laura (vineyard): which powers does she have as owner, as usufructuary, as pledgee?
cards.back:
Owner: cultivate and sell.
USUSFRUCTUS: only cultivate (fruits), not sell.
PIGNUS: not cultivate, but under certain circumstances sell.
• The extent of control over the thing depends on the type of right.
cards.old_front: Beispiel Laura (Weingarten): Welche Befugnisse hat sie als Eigentümerin, als Fruchtnießerin, als Pfandgläubigerin?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Introduction: legal subjects, things, property rights
cards.front: What are EMPHYTEUSIS and SUPERFICIES?
cards.back:
EMPHYTEUSIS = hereditary (emphyteutic) lease: the right to cultivate another's land for one's own profit, heritable.
SUPERFICIES = hereditary building right: the right to erect and maintain a building on another's land, heritable.
cards.old_front: Was sind EMPHYTEUSIS und SUPERFICIES?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What is possession (POSSESSIO)?
cards.back:
Factual control over a thing, coupled with the intention to control it.
• Possession is a fact, not a right: it only says who actually has the thing in his power.
• Elements: ANIMUS + CORPUS.
cards.old_front: Was ist Besitz (POSSESSIO)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Possession vs ownership — what is the difference?
cards.back:
The possessor HAS the thing in his power (fact); the owner is ENTITLED to have it (right).
• It does not follow from possession that someone has a right to the thing.
• Example 1: the thief Hector acquires possession, but not ownership; so does Leander.
cards.old_front: Besitz vs Eigentum — worin liegt der Unterschied?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Which three features are typical of property rights (ch. II.A)?
cards.back:
a. They grant — limited or unlimited — enjoyment of a thing.
b. They are absolute, effective against everyone.
c. They are enforceable by ACTIONES IN REM.
cards.old_front: Welche drei Merkmale sind für dingliche Rechte typisch (Kap. II.A)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: How does Roman law protect possession — and why only provisionally?
cards.back:
Through the praetor's interdicts (possessory protection), provided certain requirements are met.
• Only provisionally, because this does not decide who has a right to the thing; that is settled only by the petitory action (ACTIO IN REM).
cards.old_front: Wie schützt das römische Recht den Besitz — und warum nur vorläufig?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What is the legal significance of possession (II.B)?
cards.back:
1. In a dispute the possessor is in the stronger position: he need only surrender the thing once the claimant has proved his right.
2. Possession is often the basis for acquiring a property right:
  a. TRADITIO from the person entitled on the basis of a valid transaction → ownership
  b. OCCUPATIO of an ownerless thing → ownership
  c. Acquisition from an unauthorised person → ownership through qualified possession over a period of time (USUCAPIO)
cards.old_front: Welche rechtliche Bedeutung hat der Besitz (II.B)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What do ANIMUS and CORPUS mean as elements of possession?
cards.back:
ANIMUS = possessory intent (ANIMUS POSSIDENDI), characterised by the intention to have the thing for oneself (ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI).
CORPUS = control over the thing.
• Whoever fulfils both with regard to a corporeal thing possesses it.
• The sources do not speak of CORPUS alone, but of CORPORE POSSIDERE.
cards.old_front: Was bedeuten ANIMUS und CORPUS als Elemente des Besitzes?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Does CORPUS require physical contact with the thing?
cards.back:
No — it suffices that the thing lies within the person's sphere of influence, so that he can exercise his control realistically and unhindered.
• Example 3: the farmer Rusticus possesses his clothes (immediate control) and the cattle on his meadow (reachable at any time).
• Paulus D 41.2.1.21 (Case 4): CORPORE ET TACTU is not needed, OCULIS ET AFFECTU suffices.
• This is why CORPUS is often described as spatial proximity.
cards.old_front: Erfordert CORPUS physischen Kontakt mit der Sache?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Language note: how are ANIMUS and CORPUS used grammatically correctly?
cards.back:
Possession is acquired/retained ANIMO ET CORPORE (ablative) — or: “through ANIMUS and CORPUS”.
• Always use Latin with the correct ending.
cards.old_front: Sprachhinweis: Wie verwendet man ANIMUS und CORPUS grammatikalisch richtig?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What is proprietary possession and what is ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI?
cards.back:
Proprietary possession = possession with the intention of having the thing for oneself.
• ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI = the intention to possess in one's own name.
• When the sources speak of POSSESSIO, they usually mean this proprietary possession.
cards.old_front: Was ist Eigenbesitz (proprietary possession) und was ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Must the possessor exercise control himself?
cards.back:
No — he can also establish and retain possession through another's control (mediate possession).
• The other person holds the thing for the possessor, but does not want to possess it in his own name.
• Example 4: Rusticus leases his field to Lea → Rusticus has ANIMUS and CORPUS through Lea → proprietary possession.
cards.old_front: Muss der Besitzer die Herrschaft selbst ausüben?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What does NATURALIS POSSESSIO (natural possession) mean?
cards.back:
Not proprietary possession, but holding a thing FOR another.
• Despite the word POSSESSIO, therefore, not possession in the technical sense.
• The holder can be a free person or a slave; the sources also say TENERE, HABERE.
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet NATURALIS POSSESSIO (natürlicher Besitz)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Who is a detentor? Which typical detentors are there?
cards.back:
A holder who is SUI IURIS (neither a slave nor in the possessor's paternal or marital power) and holds the thing for another with ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI → natural possession (detention).
• Typical: tenants, leaseholders, borrowers, depositaries, precarists.
cards.old_front: Wer ist Detentor? Welche typischen Detentoren gibt es?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What does ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI mean?
cards.back:
The intention to hold a thing for another — characterises the detentor (natural possessor).
• Opposite concept: ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI (intent of proprietary possession).
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: What is the position of persons in power (ALIENI IURIS) as holders — are they detentors?
cards.back:
No — they are not detentors but possessor's agents, the “extended arm” of their DOMINUS.
• If the holder of power makes use of this arm, he has IMMEDIATE possession.
• Example 5: the slave Achilles drives Rusticus' sheep to market → Rusticus is immediate proprietary possessor.
cards.old_front: Wie stehen Gewaltunterworfene (ALIENI IURIS) als Inhaber da — Detentoren?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Immediate vs mediate possession — when does each arise?
cards.back:
Immediate: the possessor exercises control himself or through a person in his power (possessor's agent).
Mediate: control through a detentor (SUI IURIS) → the possessor has mediate proprietary possession, the detentor immediate natural possession.
cards.old_front: Unmittelbarer vs mittelbarer Besitz — wann liegt welcher vor?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Concept, significance and types of possession
cards.front: Example 1: Clara gives the vase to Midas for safekeeping; Hector steals it. What is the position as to possession?
cards.back:
After the handover: Midas has immediate natural possession (detention) for Clara; Clara is mediate proprietary possessor (ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI, CORPUS through Midas).
• The theft ends Clara's POSSESSIO and Midas' detention.
• Hector becomes POSSESSOR: control + intention to possess in his own name (with intent to enrich himself).
cards.old_front: Beispiel 1: Clara gibt die Vase dem Midas zur Verwahrung; Hector stiehlt sie. Besitzlage?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What does CORPUS require for acquiring possession?
cards.back:
Factual control: either immediate power over the thing or a very strong possibility, bordering on certainty, of establishing physical contact.
• CORPUS can exist without touching, but never becomes a merely symbolic requirement.
cards.old_front: Was verlangt CORPUS beim Besitzerwerb?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Why do the jurists impose stricter requirements on acquiring possession than on retaining it?
cards.back:
Because acquiring possession can change the existing (ownership) relations; to avoid conflict, clear and predictable rules, recognisable to everyone, are needed.
• Once established, possession can be retained without constant, manifest proof of ANIMUS and CORPUS — sometimes even SOLO ANIMO.
cards.old_front: Warum stellen die Juristen an den Besitzerwerb strengere Anforderungen als an die Besitzerhaltung?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Can possession be transferred by symbols or documents in Roman law?
cards.back:
No. The Romans always require real factual control.
• Neither TRADITIO PER CARTAM (document) nor TRADITIO FICTA (fictive delivery) nor symbols suffice.
cards.old_front: Kann im römischen Recht Besitz durch Symbole oder Urkunden übertragen werden?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Are TRADITIO BREVI MANU and CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM genuine exceptions to the requirement of CORPUS?
cards.back:
No. They are called — somewhat inaccurately — acquisition SOLO ANIMO because consensus (ANIMUS) is in the foreground; but CORPUS is always present.
• For acquisition, CORPUS is always decisive.
cards.old_front: Sind TRADITIO BREVI MANU und CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM echte Ausnahmen vom Erfordernis des CORPUS?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Who can acquire possession in his own name? What role does legal capacity play?
cards.back:
Only someone who can form a legally relevant possessory intent, ie who has legal capacity.
• PUPILLI and FURIOSI are largely excluded; a mature PUPILLUS can exceptionally form ANIMUS POSSIDENDI himself.
• The problem arises only for persons free of power (SUI IURIS); someone in another's POTESTAS cannot possess in his own name at all.
cards.old_front: Wer kann Besitz im eigenen Namen erwerben? Welche Rolle spielt die Handlungsfähigkeit?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Paulus (Ofilius, Nerva) D 41.2.1.3 (Case 22): can a PUPILLUS acquire possession without his tutor?
cards.back:
In principle no — without a tutor, FURIOSI and PUPILLI lack legally relevant possessory intent.
• Ofilius and Nerva filius: yes, without AUCTORITAS, because possession is purely a question of fact.
• Paulus: this is to be followed if the PUPILLUS already has a certain mental maturity (INTELLECTUS).
cards.old_front: Paulus (Ofilius, Nerva) D 41.2.1.3 (Case 22): Kann ein PUPILLUS ohne Tutor Besitz erwerben?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Original vs derivative acquisition of possession — difference and examples?
cards.back:
Original: solely by one's own act, without the cooperation of the previous possessor — eg OCCUPATIO of a RES NULLIUS, but also the thief.
Derivative: with the cooperation of the previous possessor, who transfers control — TRADITIO.
• In derivative acquisition, the acquirer steps into the position of the previous possessor.
cards.old_front: Originärer vs derivativer Besitzerwerb — Unterschied und Beispiele?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What kind of possession does a thief acquire — and does he acquire ownership?
cards.back:
He acquires original possession (by his own act, without the cooperation of the previous possessor) — but never ownership.
• His possession is not based on an IUSTA CAUSA and is flawed in relation to the person robbed.
cards.old_front: Welche Art Besitz erwirbt ein Dieb — und erwirbt er Eigentum?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What is a RES NULLIUS, and what does OCCUPATIO bring about?
cards.back:
RES NULLIUS = a thing that is in nobody's possession or ownership.
• By OCCUPATIO (seizing it) one acquires possession and ownership — originally.
cards.old_front: Was ist eine RES NULLIUS, was bewirkt die OCCUPATIO?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: How is ANIMUS POSSIDENDI expressed?
cards.back:
Expressly (eg the buyer declares that he now wants to take possession) or — usually — implicitly through conduct aimed at establishing or exercising control.
• The hunter (OCCUPATIO) and the thief (FURTUM) do not speak, but their purposeful conduct clearly shows possessory intent.
cards.old_front: Wie wird ANIMUS POSSIDENDI geäußert?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Contract vs conveyance — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Contract: creates the obligation to transfer; gives the creditor a claim against the debtor to DARE, FACERE, PRAESTARE. It is the agreement on the ground (causa) of a conveyance.
Conveyance (transfer of the right itself, transfer of title): a legal act that changes the scope or attribution of a right — usually by delivery of possession (TRADITIO).
cards.old_front: Vertrag vs Verfügung (contract vs conveyance) — Unterschied?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: When is the EMPTIO VENDITIO concluded — and does the buyer thereby acquire possession or ownership?
cards.back:
As soon as there is agreement on goods and price (consensual contract; no document, no exchange needed).
• The buyer thereby acquires neither possession nor ownership; the sale only creates obligations (delivery or payment).
• Only performance by TRADITIO (conveyance) transfers.
cards.old_front: Wann ist die EMPTIO VENDITIO geschlossen — und erwirbt der Käufer dadurch Besitz oder Eigentum?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Is the intention to buy already ANIMUS POSSIDENDI?
cards.back:
No. The intention to be a contracting party (to buy) and the intention to acquire possession by conveyance must be strictly separated — only the latter is ANIMUS POSSIDENDI.
• Example 10: Leo buys a cart on 1 March, Melitta delivers on 15 March → contract on 1 March, transfer of possession only on 15 March.
• Purpose: the buyer may want delivery later, eg for storage reasons.
cards.old_front: Ist der Kaufwille schon ANIMUS POSSIDENDI?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What is required of the parties for a TRADITIO?
cards.back:
An agreement that the delivery is to transfer possession; on the acquirer's side it is expressed in the ANIMUS POSSIDENDI.
• In a conveyance by TRADITIO, the acquisition of possession is part of the transfer.
cards.old_front: Was ist für eine TRADITIO auf Seiten der Parteien erforderlich?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Ulpianus (Trebatius, Labeo) D 18.6.1.2 (Case 11): the buyer seals a particular wine barrel in the seller's cellar. Does he acquire possession of the wine?
cards.back:
Disputed — according to the prevailing (later) view, no.
• Trebatius (late Republic): yes — the sealing clearly shows ANIMUS POSSIDENDI.
• Labeo (early classical) and Ulpian (late classical): no — the seal is only meant to prevent later substitution and shows no present possessory intent.
• CORPUS is unproblematic (the buyer is at the barrel and touches it).
cards.old_front: Ulpianus (Trebatius, Labeo) D 18.6.1.2 (Case 11): Der Käufer versiegelt im Keller des Verkäufers ein bestimmtes Weinfass. Erwirbt er Besitz am Wein?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: How does the textbook explain the different assessment of sealing by Trebatius and Labeo/Ulpian (D 18.6.1.2)?
cards.back:
Not as deliberate casuistry, but from the context: in Trebatius' time sealing was probably a commercial custom to express possessory intent; later it was understood as a mere selection of the goods.
• Since transfer of possession (with IUSTA CAUSA and power of disposal) also transfers ownership, Labeo perhaps did not yet want ownership to pass.
cards.old_front: Wie erklärt das Lehrbuch die unterschiedliche Bewertung des Versiegelns bei Trebatius bzw Labeo/Ulpian (D 18.6.1.2)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Paulus (Alfenus) D 18.6.15(14).1 (Case 7): the buyer marks wooden beams in the seller's storehouse. Acquisition of possession?
cards.back:
Yes — Alfenus and Paulus: the buyer acquires possession of the marked beams.
• Marking counts as a clear expression of ANIMUS POSSIDENDI — probably a uniform custom of timber merchants; generally recognised.
• Contrast with sealing the wine barrel (D 18.6.1.2), which according to Labeo/Ulpian does not suffice.
cards.old_front: Paulus (Alfenus) D 18.6.15(14).1 (Case 7): Der Käufer markiert im Lager des Verkäufers Holzbalken. Besitzerwerb?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What is IUS CONTROVERSUM, and when is there a genuine controversy?
cards.back:
Opposing juristic opinions are equally part of Roman law (IUS CONTROVERSUM).
• A genuine controversy exists only where views are opposed on the same case/type of case — not where the solutions are explained by different facts or a later jurist criticises outdated opinions.
cards.old_front: Was ist IUS CONTROVERSUM, und wann spricht man von einer echten Kontroverse?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: According to the textbook, which factors determine the degree of CORPUS required for acquiring possession?
cards.back:
1. Derivative vs original: derivative acquisition requires less control (stepping into an established position).
2. Immovable vs movable: land cannot disappear → easier to control.
3. External form: small, handy things are easier to control than large, inaccessible stores of goods.
4. Social environment: high risk of interference by third parties → a manifest act of control (seizing) is needed; calm environment → a realistic possibility of access suffices.
cards.old_front: Von welchen Faktoren hängt nach dem Lehrbuch das Maß an CORPUS beim Besitzerwerb ab?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What are immovable things? Is a heavy, bulky thing immovable?
cards.back:
Immovable: land and everything firmly attached to it (buildings with a solid foundation, rooted plants).
• Everything else is movable — even if it is heavy and bulky.
• No FURTUM is possible in respect of immovable things.
cards.old_front: Was sind unbewegliche Sachen? Ist eine schwere, sperrige Sache unbeweglich?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What role does the social environment play in acquiring possession?
cards.back:
Where there is a high risk of interference by third parties (eg a busy market), the jurists tend to require a manifest act of control, such as seizing with the hand.
• In an orderly environment with little conflict, CORPUS can already exist with the realistic possibility of access.
cards.old_front: Welche Rolle spielt das soziale Umfeld beim Besitzerwerb?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Paulus D 41.2.3.1 (Case 1): how does one acquire possession of land?
cards.back:
One need not walk round all of it; it suffices to set foot on it with the intention to acquire.
• In principle, setting foot on it is required.
cards.old_front: Paulus D 41.2.3.1 (Case 1): Wie erwirbt man Besitz an einem Grundstück?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Celsus D 41.2.18.2 (2nd sentence) (Case 2): the seller shows the buyer the land from the buyer's own tower. Acquisition of possession?
cards.back:
Yes — the buyer acquires possession if the seller, with the intention to transfer, shows the land from the tower on the buyer's neighbouring estate.
• Borderline case: decisive is that the buyer already possesses the neighbouring land and can extend his sphere of influence to the land to be acquired.
cards.old_front: Celsus D 41.2.18.2 (2. Satz) (Case 2): Der Verkäufer zeigt dem Käufer das Grundstück von dessen eigenem Turm aus. Besitzerwerb?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Celsus D 41.2.18.2 (1st sentence) (Case 2): as agreed, B is to place the purchased goods in A's house; nobody is there. Acquisition of possession?
cards.back:
Yes — with delivery in the house, A has CORPUS; his ANIMUS follows from the agreement.
• Not a case of OCULIS ET AFFECTU: A wants to possess only on arrival in the house, and the agreement was not made in the presence of the goods.
cards.old_front: Celsus D 41.2.18.2 (1. Satz) (Case 2): B soll die gekaufte Ware vereinbarungsgemäß in A's Haus stellen; niemand ist dort. Besitzerwerb?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Iavolenus D 46.3.79 (Case 3): C is to give D money/goods; at D's direction, C lays them down in front of D. Does D acquire possession although he does not touch them?
cards.back:
Yes — as soon as C, at D's direction, lays the thing down in front of him, it comes under D's control and into his possession.
• CORPUS = possibility of taking physical control; no seizing needed.
• Romans: QUODAMMODO MANU LONGA TRADITA (“as if delivered by a long hand”).
cards.old_front: Iavolenus D 46.3.79 (Case 3): C soll D Geld/Waren leisten; auf D's Anordnung legt C sie vor D hin. Erwirbt D Besitz, obwohl er sie nicht berührt?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What does “LONGA MANU TRADITIO” mean — is it a clearly defined legal institution?
cards.back:
With QUODAMMODO MANU LONGA TRADITA the Romans explain all cases in which possession passes without a physical act of seizing by the recipient (CORPUS = possibility of access).
• Because the cases differ, it is not a clearly defined legal institution.
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet „LONGA MANU TRADITIO“ — ist sie ein fest umrissenes Rechtsinstitut?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: What does acquiring possession OCULIS ET AFFECTU mean (Paulus D 41.2.1.21, Case 4)?
cards.back:
If buyer and seller agree, in the presence of the goods, on the immediate transfer of possession, the buyer acquires possession without any further act.
• Physical control (CORPORE ET TACTU) is unnecessary: it suffices that the thing has come within his field of vision and his sphere of control.
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet Besitzerwerb OCULIS ET AFFECTU (Paulus D 41.2.1.21, Case 4)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Which four cases of acquiring possession OCULIS ET AFFECTU does Paulus D 41.2.1.21 (Case 4) mention?
cards.back:
1. In the presence of the goods, buyer and seller agree on delivery to the buyer's PROCURATOR.
2. Debtor and creditor agree, in the presence of the coins owed, that the debtor will pay them to a third party.
3. With an extraordinarily heavy thing, buyer and seller agree in its presence on the transfer of possession.
4. The seller hands the wine buyer the keys to the cellar in which the wine is stored.
cards.old_front: Welche vier Fälle des Besitzerwerbs OCULIS ET AFFECTU nennt Paulus D 41.2.1.21 (Case 4)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Paulus D 41.2.1.21, 2nd case: debtor and creditor agree, in the presence of the coins, that the debtor will hand them to a third party. Legal consequences?
cards.back:
Through the agreement in the presence of the money, the creditor acquires possession of the coins and the debtor is released.
• If the debtor later delivers the money to the third party, he holds it in the creditor's name (as his holder).
cards.old_front: Paulus D 41.2.1.21, 2. Fall: Schuldner und Gläubiger vereinbaren in Gegenwart der Münzen, dass der Schuldner sie einem Dritten übergibt. Rechtsfolgen?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Paulus D 41.2.1.21, 1st case (delivery to the PROCURATOR): must the procurator be present at the agreement?
cards.back: No — on a consistent reading as acquisition OCULIS ET AFFECTU, the buyer acquires already with the agreement in the presence of the goods; the procurator is only to collect the goods later and need not be present.
cards.old_front: Paulus D 41.2.1.21, 1. Fall (Lieferung an den PROCURATOR): Muss der Procurator bei der Vereinbarung anwesend sein?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Handing over the keys of the wine cellar (Paulus D 41.2.1.21, 4th case): under what condition does it fit acquisition OCULIS ET AFFECTU?
cards.back: Only if one imagines that the keys are handed over at the wine cellar (in the presence of the goods).
cards.old_front: Schlüsselübergabe beim Weinkeller (Paulus D 41.2.1.21, 4. Fall): Unter welcher Voraussetzung passt sie zum Erwerb OCULIS ET AFFECTU?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Papinianus D 18.1.74 (Case 5): when does the buyer of goods in a warehouse acquire possession?
cards.back: As soon as the keys are handed over to him — provided the handover takes place at the warehouse.
cards.old_front: Papinianus D 18.1.74 (Case 5): Wann erwirbt der Käufer von Waren in einem Lagerhaus Besitz?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Gaius D 41.1.9.6 (Case 6): possession (and ownership) of stored goods by handing over keys — which two readings are possible?
cards.back:
1. The text tacitly presupposes handover near the goods → as in Papinian D 18.1.74.
2. The keys themselves provide sufficient CORPUS, wherever handed over — if the store is securely locked and the keys are the only means of access (apart from force).
• Gaius does not say expressly that the handover must take place at the store.
cards.old_front: Gaius D 41.1.9.6 (Case 6): Besitz (und Eigentum) an Lagerware durch Schlüsselübergabe — welche zwei Deutungen sind möglich?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Gaius (Trebatius) D 41.1.5.1 (Case 8): a hunter has wounded a wild animal so that it can be caught. Is he possessor (and owner)?
cards.back:
Controversial — Gaius (prevailing): no, only once he actually catches it.
• Trebatius: yes, as soon as it is wounded so as to be catchable and as long as he pursues it.
• Gaius: QUIA MULTA ACCIDERE POSSUNT, UT EAM NON CAPIAMUS — many things can still prevent its capture.
cards.old_front: Gaius (Trebatius) D 41.1.5.1 (Case 8): Ein Jäger hat ein wildes Tier so verwundet, dass es gefangen werden kann. Ist er Besitzer (und Eigentümer)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Proculus D 41.1.55 (Case 9): a wild boar is caught in the hunter's trap; a third party sets it free. Has the hunter acquired possession (and ownership)?
cards.back:
Proculus gives no fixed criterion — only: SI IN MEAM POTESTATEM PERVENIT, MEUS FACTUS SIT (only once it has come into my power).
• 1. Does the trap give lasting control? If the animal can free itself after a long struggle → no CORPUS.
• 2. Risk of interference by third parties: greater on public land or another's land against the owner's will; smaller with his consent or on one's own land.
cards.old_front: Proculus D 41.1.55 (Case 9): Ein Wildschwein ist in der Falle des Jägers gefangen; ein Dritter lässt es frei. Hat der Jäger Besitz (und Eigentum) erworben?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquiring possession: principles, ANIMUS, CORPUS
cards.front: Why do the hunting cases (D 41.1.5.1, D 41.1.55) take a rather strict view of CORPUS?
cards.back: Because they concern original acquisition of possession: the possessory position must be newly created, hence stricter requirements than for derivative acquisition.
cards.old_front: Warum vertreten die Jagdfälle (D 41.1.5.1, D 41.1.55) eher strenge Anforderungen an CORPUS?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What is TRADITIO BREVI MANU?
cards.back:
Acquisition of possession by the detentor by virtue of an agreement with the possessor: the possessor gives up his ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI, and with his permission the detentor henceforth holds the thing in his own name.
• The acquirer already has CORPUS as the former detentor.
cards.old_front: Was ist TRADITIO BREVI MANU?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Gaius D 41.1.9.5 (Case 12): B is borrower/tenant/depositary of a thing belonging to A; then they make a sale. Must B return the thing so that A can deliver it to him?
cards.back:
No — the agreement that the thing remains with the buyer B suffices (TRADITIO BREVI MANU).
• Since the sale is the causa and A is evidently the owner, B acquires possession AND ownership.
cards.old_front: Gaius D 41.1.9.5 (Case 12): B ist Entlehner/Mieter/Verwahrer einer Sache des A; dann kaufen sie. Muss B die Sache zurückgeben, damit A sie ihm übergeben kann?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What is a CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM?
cards.back:
Acquisition of possession by agreement: someone forms ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI for a thing he does not possess and agrees that the possessor (or detentor) will henceforth hold it in his name.
• The acquirer does not have the thing in his hands and acquires only mediate possession.
cards.old_front: Was ist ein CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: TRADITIO BREVI MANU vs CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM — what is the difference?
cards.back:
BREVI MANU: the former detentor becomes possessor (the thing is already with him).
CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM: the former possessor becomes the acquirer's detentor (the thing stays with him; the acquirer receives mediate possession).
• Both rest on consensus; without any outwardly visible giving and taking (“tradition surrogates”).
cards.old_front: TRADITIO BREVI MANU vs CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM — Unterschied?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Ulpianus D 6.1.77 (Case 20): a woman writes to a man (not her husband) that she donates a piece of land to him but wants to hold it henceforth as his tenant. How does he acquire possession — (1) if he is not on the land, (2) if he is there?
cards.back:
(1) By CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM: the donation shows his intention to acquire; in the lease she declares that she holds the land in his name → mediate possession.
(2) If he is already on the land, he has immediate possession through his presence; the lease and her role as detentor are irrelevant for acquiring possession.
• “Not her husband”: donations between spouses are void.
• His acceptance is not mentioned in the text — probably agreed beforehand.
cards.old_front: Ulpianus D 6.1.77 (Case 20): Eine Frau schreibt einem Mann (nicht ihrem Ehemann), sie schenke ihm ein Grundstück, wolle es aber künftig als seine Mieterin halten. Wie erwirbt er Besitz — (1) wenn er nicht auf dem Grundstück ist, (2) wenn er dort ist?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Iavolenus D 41.2.21.3 (Case 19): A asks B for a PRECARIUM (believing B to be the owner); later A learns that the thing belongs to C and leases it from C. Position as to possession?
cards.back:
At first A is detentor for B. Through the LOCATIO CONDUCTIO A becomes C's detentor: C expresses his possessory intent, A acknowledges it → C acquires possession through A, who exercises CORPUS for him.
• If B consents → derivative acquisition by C; if A acts without B → original acquisition by C.
• Alternatively: A first acquires possession himself and transfers it to C by CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM.
cards.old_front: Iavolenus D 41.2.21.3 (Case 19): A erbittet von B ein PRECARIUM (glaubt B ist Eigentümer); später erfährt A, dass die Sache C gehört, und mietet sie von C. Besitzlage?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What is a PRECARIUM?
cards.back:
A gratuitous grant of the use of a thing upon entreaty, revocable at any time (grant upon entreaty).
• For the Romans a factual relationship, not a contract (unlike the loan, from which both sides have ACTIONES IN PERSONAM).
• The precarist is a detentor.
cards.old_front: Was ist ein PRECARIUM?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What does NEMO SIBI IPSE CAUSAM POSSESSIONIS MUTARE POTEST mean?
cards.back:
Nobody can change the legal ground of his possession of his own accord.
• Whoever declares himself possessor has no IUSTA CAUSA POSSESSIONIS → none of the advantages of civil possession (eg no usucaption).
• Applies to the FUR and to the detentor who unilaterally wants to possess in his own name.
• Exceptions: OCCUPATIO of ownerless things, USUCAPIO PRO HEREDE. Cf § 319 ABGB.
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet NEMO SIBI IPSE CAUSAM POSSESSIONIS MUTARE POTEST?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Do TRADITIO BREVI MANU and CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM violate NEMO SIBI IPSE CAUSAM POSSESSIONIS MUTARE POTEST?
cards.back:
No — they rest on the agreement of BOTH parties, not on a unilateral change.
• Possible rationale of the rule: the justification of the acquisition of possession was shown in the TRADITIO; if a manifest act is missing, unlawful possession is suspected.
cards.old_front: Verstoßen TRADITIO BREVI MANU und CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM gegen NEMO SIBI IPSE CAUSAM POSSESSIONIS MUTARE POTEST?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Why are TRADITIO BREVI MANU and CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM called “tradition surrogates”?
cards.back: Because they are not a TRADITIO in the sense of a physical act of delivery, yet they transfer possession — without any giving and taking visible to outsiders.
cards.old_front: Warum heißen TRADITIO BREVI MANU und CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM „Traditionssurrogate“?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Can persons in power (ALIENI IURIS) acquire possession?
cards.back:
Not in their own name (incapable of holding property), but they can in the name of their DOMINUS.
• ALIENI IURIS: FILII/FILIAE FAMILIAS, UXORES IN MANU (paternal power), SERVI/SERVAE (the owner's power).
• Paulus: possession is acquired ANIMO NOSTRO, CORPORE ALIENO.
cards.old_front: Können Gewaltunterworfene (ALIENI IURIS) Besitz erwerben?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What does ANIMO NOSTRO, CORPORE ALIENO mean?
cards.back:
Acquisition through persons in power: the DOMINUS has the ANIMUS, the person in power establishes the CORPUS (he himself does not act physically).
• Paulus D 41.2.3.12 (Case 24).
cards.old_front: Was bedeutet ANIMO NOSTRO, CORPORE ALIENO?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What does the DOMINUS' CORPUS consist of when he acquires through persons in power?
cards.back:
1. The relationship of power (POTESTAS), which makes the persons in power his “extended arm”.
2. The factual control of the person in power over the thing.
• To acquire through a slave, the DOMINUS must himself possess the slave (exception: usufructuary, Gai Inst 2.94).
• Children of the house are not possessed; the basis is the PATRIA POTESTAS.
cards.old_front: Woraus besteht das CORPUS des DOMINUS beim Erwerb durch Gewaltunterworfene?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: In which two ways can the DOMINUS express his ANIMUS when acquiring through persons in power?
cards.back:
a. IUSSUM: an order for one particular transaction.
b. PECULIUM: a general authorisation to acquire possession within the scope of the PECULIUM — the possessory intent is expressed in general, abstract terms.
cards.old_front: Auf welche zwei Arten kann der DOMINUS seinen ANIMUS beim Erwerb durch Gewaltunterworfene äußern?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What is a PECULIUM and what is its significance for acquiring possession?
cards.back:
Assets that the DOMINUS leaves to a person in his power for independent management (in organisational terms: a branch).
• Whatever the holder of the PECULIUM acquires in his transactions, he acquires for the DOMINUS.
• The authorisation covers ALL of the holder's transactions, not only those typical of the branch.
• The ANIMUS is concretised by the holder for each transaction → acquisition ANIMO SERVORUM.
cards.old_front: Was ist ein PECULIUM und welche Bedeutung hat es für den Besitzerwerb?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What applies if a person in power accepts a thing without a IUSSUM and without a PECULIUM?
cards.back:
Then the DOMINUS acquires no possession — only with a IUSSUM or PECULIUM.
• If the DOMINUS approves after the fact (RATIHABITIO), this is treated as if he had given a IUSSUM beforehand (cf Ulpian D 46.3.12.4: RATI ENIM HABITIO MANDATO COMPARATUR).
cards.old_front: Was gilt, wenn ein Gewaltunterworfener ohne IUSSUM und ohne PECULIUM eine Sache annimmt?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: When acquiring through a person in power, does that person's own intention matter?
cards.back:
No — he need only establish CORPUS; whether he has ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI is irrelevant. He acquires for the DOMINUS even if he wants to possess himself.
• Only INTELLECTUS POSSIDENDI is required → even under-age persons in power with sufficient understanding can acquire.
cards.old_front: Kommt es beim Erwerb durch einen Gewaltunterworfenen auf dessen eigenen Willen an?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Papinianus D 41.2.48 (Case 21): by letter, A donates to B an estate together with the slaves living there; one slave comes to B, B sends him back. When does B acquire possession?
cards.back:
Letter and acceptance alone do not change possession.
• Of the slave who comes to him: CORPORE ET ANIMO.
• If B sends him back with the IUSSUM to take over the estate and the slaves, B acquires possession of them ANIMO NOSTRO CORPORE ALIENO (as soon as the slave takes control there).
cards.old_front: Papinianus D 41.2.48 (Case 21): A schenkt B brieflich ein Gut samt den dort lebenden Sklaven; ein Sklave kommt zu B, B schickt ihn zurück. Wann erwirbt B Besitz?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Paulus (Sabinus, Cassius, Iulianus) D 41.2.1.5 (Case 25): must the DOMINUS know of the individual transactions within the PECULIUM?
cards.back:
No — because of the general authorisation he acquires possession even without knowledge.
• Even persons who did not grant the PECULIUM themselves (and could not revoke it for lack of legal capacity) acquire in this way: the INFANS (the father granted it before his death), the FURIOSUS (granted it while of sound mind), the HERES (inherits a slave with a PECULIUM).
cards.old_front: Paulus (Sabinus, Cassius, Iulianus) D 41.2.1.5 (Case 25): Muss der DOMINUS von den einzelnen Geschäften im Rahmen des PECULIUM wissen?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Could persons free of power (SUI IURIS) acquire possession for another in pre-classical and classical law?
cards.back:
In principle no (Gai Inst 2.95, Paul Sent 5.2.2) — no direct agency in acquiring possession.
• Example 11: Secunda buys from Tertius for Primus → Secunda becomes possessor and then transfers to Primus in a separate act (today: indirect agency).
• Transferring possession, on the other hand, was always possible through an authorised person free of power.
cards.old_front: Können Gewaltfreie (SUI IURIS) im vorklassischen und klassischen Recht Besitz für einen anderen erwerben?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Direct vs indirect agency in acquiring possession — what is the difference?
cards.back:
Direct: the agent's transaction takes effect immediately for the principal; possession passes directly from the alienor to him.
Indirect: two transactions — the agent himself acquires possession and then transfers it to the principal.
cards.old_front: Direkte vs indirekte Stellvertretung beim Besitzerwerb — Unterschied?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Which persons free of power can exceptionally acquire possession as direct agents?
cards.back:
a. CURATOR — for the mentally disabled person/spendthrift in his care
b. TUTOR — for his ward
c. PROCURATOR (manager) — for his master
• Reason for the PROCURATOR: dependence on the DOMINUS (often his freedman) → acquisition as through a slave.
• Justinian (6th century) opens up direct agency in acquiring possession generally.
cards.old_front: Welche Gewaltfreien können ausnahmsweise als direkte Stellvertreter Besitz erwerben?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: Ulpianus D 41.1.20.2 (Case 36): Titius and Ego buy jointly; only Titius is present at the delivery and also accepts for Ego. Who acquires possession?
cards.back:
Both acquire possession simultaneously with the delivery to Titius.
• Titius acts for Ego “as if a PROCURATOR” (TITIO ET QUASI MEO PROCURATORI TRADITA; Ulpian cautiously: PUTO) — analogy.
• The reasoning QUIA PLACET PER LIBERAM PERSONAM … is probably a Justinianic interpolation.
cards.old_front: Ulpianus D 41.1.20.2 (Case 36): Titius und Ego kaufen gemeinsam; nur Titius ist bei der Übergabe und nimmt auch für Ego entgegen. Wer erwirbt Besitz?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: What is an analogy (using the example of D 41.1.20.2)?
cards.back: Solving a legal problem that does not exactly show the features of a recognised case but is regarded as similar — here: Titius is treated like a PROCURATOR although he is not one.
cards.old_front: Was ist eine Analogie (am Beispiel von D 41.1.20.2)?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Acquisition SOLO ANIMO; through persons in power and agents
cards.front: How does acquisition of possession through third parties differ in classical law (up to the early 3rd century) from Justinianic law (early 6th century)?
cards.back:
Classical: persons free of power can in principle not acquire directly for others (only indirectly; exceptions tutor, curator, procurator); acquisition through persons in power with IUSSUM/PECULIUM.
Justinian: direct agency in acquiring possession is possible also through free persons (QUA PLACET PER LIBERAM PERSONAM).

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 1a] On 1 January Ago tries out the stallion Pegasus at Bellona's stud farm. On 3 January he buys it at the market for 6,000 and pays 1,000 down. On 9 January Bellona delivers Pegasus; Ago pays the rest on 15 January. When does Ago acquire possession?
cards.back:
On 9 January with the delivery (TRADITIO) — derivative acquisition of possession.
• 1 January test ride: no ANIMUS POSSIDENDI (only testing), no acquisition of possession.
• 3 January contract of sale (agreement on goods and price) + down payment: only creates obligations; intention to buy ≠ possessory intent; no CORPUS.
• Payment of the price on 15 January is irrelevant for possession.
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 1a] Ago probiert am 1.1. auf Bellonas Gestüt den Hengst Pegasus aus. Am 3.1. kauft er ihn auf dem Markt um 6.000 und zahlt 1.000 an. Am 9.1. übergibt Bellona Pegasus; den Rest zahlt Ago am 15.1. Wann erwirbt Ago Besitz?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 1b] On 3 January Ago buys Bellona's stallion Pegasus. When he wants to collect it on 9 January, Pegasus has disappeared: Hermes stole it the night before and is hiding it in his stable. Position as to possession?
cards.back:
Ago never acquires possession; Bellona loses it through the theft; Hermes has original possession.
• The sale gives Ago no possession; no delivery took place.
• Hermes commits FURTUM and acquires possession by his own act (ANIMUS REM SIBI HABENDI + CORPUS), but not ownership.

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 2] Brontes and his neighbour Clara inspect Brontes' meadow. The next day, on the balcony of Clara's villa, which borders the meadow and from which the meadow is clearly visible, they agree on 17,000; Brontes declares that he now gives her possession, Clara agrees. Clara sets foot on the meadow only a week later. When and how does Clara acquire possession?
cards.back:
At the moment of the agreement on the balcony — without setting foot on it.
• In principle one must set foot on land (Paulus D 41.2.3.1, Case 1).
• Celsus D 41.2.18.2 (Case 2, tower): if the seller, with the intention to transfer, shows the land from the buyer's neighbouring estate, the buyer acquires possession — because he can extend his sphere of influence onto it from the neighbouring land he already possesses.
• Inspection on the previous day: neither ANIMUS nor CORPUS. Setting foot on it later is irrelevant.
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 2] Brontes und seine Nachbarin Clara besichtigen Brontes' Wiese. Am nächsten Tag einigen sie sich auf dem Balkon von Claras Villa, die an die Wiese grenzt und von der man die Wiese gut sieht, auf 17.000; Brontes erklärt, er überlasse ihr jetzt den Besitz, Clara ist einverstanden. Erst nach einer Woche betritt Clara die Wiese. Wann und wie erwirbt Clara Besitz?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 3] The amateur hunter Dexter digs a deep pit at a remote spot in Eros' large forest to catch game. A stag falls in, breaks its neck and dies. Arguments for and against Dexter's acquisition of possession?
cards.back:
No clear result — it depends on CORPUS (ANIMUS is given by the intention to catch).
• For: the dead stag can no longer free itself → lasting control through the pit (Proculus D 41.1.55, Case 9); the spot is remote (low risk of interference).
• Against: another's land (consent by Eros is not mentioned) → increased risk of interference by third parties; Dexter is not present and has not seized the animal; in original acquisition the requirements are strict (Gaius D 41.1.5.1, Case 8: only with actual capture).
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 3] Der Hobbyjäger Dexter gräbt an einer abgelegenen Stelle im großen Wald des Eros eine tiefe Grube, um Wild zu fangen. Ein Hirsch stürzt hinein, bricht sich das Genick und stirbt. Argumente für und gegen Dexters Besitzerwerb?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 4a] On payday the trader Cassandra lays the money down in front of Felix; Felix does not pick it up, gives her a receipt and asks her to take the money to the shipowner Merops, to whom he owes money. On the way, robbers steal the money. Who possesses the money in the course of events?
cards.back:
1. Felix acquires possession as soon as Cassandra lays the money down in front of him — without touching it (Iavolenus D 46.3.79, Case 3: QUODAMMODO MANU LONGA TRADITA).
2. With the instruction to take it to Merops, Cassandra becomes Felix's detentor (ANIMUS REM ALTERI HABENDI); Felix has mediate proprietary possession (cf Paulus D 41.2.1.21, case 2: the debtor then holds the coins in the creditor's name).
3. The robbers acquire original possession through FURTUM; Felix loses it.
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 4a] Die Händlerin Cassandra legt Felix am Zahltag das Geld vor ihm hin; Felix nimmt es nicht auf, gibt ihr eine Quittung und bittet sie, das Geld dem Reeder Merops zu bringen, dem er Geld schuldet. Unterwegs rauben Räuber das Geld. Wer besitzt das Geld im Laufe der Ereignisse?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 4b] Variant: Cassandra is to take Felix's money to the shipowner Merops, finds Merops asleep on the veranda and puts the money and a note on the table beside him. Before he wakes up, unknown persons steal the money. Who had possession?
cards.back:
Merops acquires no possession: he is asleep and knows nothing of the money → no ANIMUS (nor is the money within his conscious control).
• Whether Felix (through Cassandra) remains possessor is disputed: according to one view, the transferor gives up possession only on condition that the recipient acquires it (Ulpian D 41.2.34 pr, Case 44) → Felix remains possessor; according to another view, he gives it up in any event → the money is without a possessor (Celsus D 41.2.18.1, Case 43).
• The thieves acquire original possession.
• (In b the book writes “When Felix wakes up” — evidently Merops is meant.)
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 4b] Variante: Cassandra soll Felix' Geld dem Reeder Merops bringen, findet Merops schlafend auf der Veranda und legt Geld und eine Notiz neben ihn auf den Tisch. Bevor er aufwacht, stehlen Unbekannte das Geld. Wer hatte Besitz?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 5] Gripus buys 50 measures of olive oil from Helena; in her cellar, in her presence and with her consent, he seals five amphorae of ten measures each and declares: “This oil now belongs to me; I will soon send someone to collect it.” At night the amphorae break in an earthquake. Has Gripus acquired possession of the amphorae and the oil?
cards.back:
Yes, with his declaration — but possession ends when the amphorae and the oil perish in the earthquake.
• CORPUS: present, touches the amphorae; agreement on immediate transfer in the presence of the goods (OCULIS ET AFFECTU, Paulus D 41.2.1.21).
• ANIMUS: according to Labeo/Ulpian (D 18.6.1.2) sealing alone does not suffice — but here there is an express declaration.
• That he has the goods collected only later does no harm: Helena then holds them for him.
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 5] Gripus kauft von Helena 50 Maß Olivenöl, versiegelt in ihrem Keller in ihrer Gegenwart und mit ihrer Zustimmung fünf Amphoren zu je zehn Maß und erklärt: „Dieses Öl gehört jetzt mir; ich schicke bald jemanden, um es zu holen.“ Nachts zerbrechen die Amphoren bei einem Erdbeben. Hat Gripus Besitz an Amphoren und Öl erworben?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 9] Agatha has bought a riding horse from Brontes and orders her slave Carus to collect it. Carus collects it and leads it into Agatha's stable; the next day Agatha rides it for the first time. When does Agatha acquire possession?
cards.back:
As soon as Carus takes over the horse at Brontes' — ANIMO NOSTRO, CORPORE ALIENO.
• Agatha's ANIMUS lies in the IUSSUM (order for this transaction); CORPUS is established by her slave, her “extended arm”.
• Neither stabling the horse nor the first ride is decisive.
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 9] Agatha hat bei Brontes ein Reitpferd gekauft und befiehlt ihrem Sklaven Carus, es zu holen. Carus holt es und führt es in Agathas Stall; am nächsten Tag reitet Agatha es zum ersten Mal. Wann erwirbt Agatha Besitz?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 10] Carus sends his slave Leandros, manager of his theatre in Pompeii, with a letter to Berenike in Rome: he donates Leandros and the theatre to her. Berenike gives Leandros instructions and sends him back to run the theatre for her henceforth; two days later Leandros tells the theatre slaves that he now manages it for Berenike. When does Berenike acquire possession of (a) Leandros, (b) the theatre, (c) the other slaves?
cards.back:
As in Papinian D 41.2.48 (Case 21): letter and acceptance alone do not change possession.
(a) Leandros: when he is with her and she takes him over with instructions — CORPORE ET ANIMO.
(b) Theatre and (c) other slaves: when Leandros arrives in Pompeii two days later and takes control for her — ANIMO NOSTRO CORPORE ALIENO (her IUSSUM = ANIMUS, Leandros establishes CORPUS).
• Prerequisite: she herself possesses Leandros.
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 10] Carus schickt seinen Sklaven Leandros, Verwalter seines Theaters in Pompeji, mit einem Brief zu Berenike nach Rom: Er schenke ihr Leandros und das Theater. Berenike gibt Leandros Anweisungen und schickt ihn zurück, um das Theater künftig für sie zu führen; zwei Tage später sagt Leandros den Theatersklaven, er leite es nun für Berenike. Wann erwirbt Berenike Besitz an (a) Leandros, (b) dem Theater, (c) den übrigen Sklaven?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 12] The wholesale grain dealer Leo has his Naples branch run by his slave Melitta with a PECULIUM. On 1 April Melitta buys a ton of grain, which Xerxes is still expecting by ship. Three days later, with PECULIUM money, she buys a tunic for herself from the tailor Helena. Who possesses the grain and the tunic?
cards.back:
Grain: nobody from Leo's household — it has only been bought, not yet delivered (sale ≠ possession); the seller remains possessor until delivery.
Tunic: Leo — with the delivery to Melitta.
• The PECULIUM authorises acquisition for the DOMINUS in general, for ALL of the holder's transactions, not only those typical of the branch.
• Melitta's intention to have the tunic for herself is irrelevant; Leo need not know of the purchase (Paulus D 41.2.1.5).
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 12] Getreidegroßhändler Leo lässt seine Filiale in Neapel von seiner Sklavin Melitta mit PECULIUM führen. Am 1.4. kauft Melitta eine Tonne Getreide, das Xerxes erst per Schiff erwartet. Drei Tage später kauft sie mit Peculiumsgeld beim Schneider Helena eine Tunika für sich. Wer besitzt Getreide und Tunika?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 15a] Japyx asks Cassandra to buy Argos' villa for him at an auction in Capri. Cassandra makes the winning bid and inspects it in person a week later. Shortly afterwards she asks Japyx whether she may rent the villa for the summer; Japyx agrees. In autumn Japyx visits the villa for the first time with his slaves. Who possesses the villa, and how?
cards.back:
1. Winning bid (sale): no possession.
2. Inspection: Cassandra acquires possession in her OWN name by setting foot on it (Paulus D 41.2.3.1) — as a person free of power she cannot acquire directly for Japyx in classical law; she is neither tutor, curator nor procurator (indirect agency).
3. Lease: Cassandra acknowledges Japyx as possessor and henceforth holds the villa for him → Japyx acquires mediate possession, Cassandra becomes detentor (CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM; cf Case 19).
4. Autumn: Japyx himself exercises immediate control with his slaves.
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 15a] Japyx bittet Cassandra, für ihn auf einer Versteigerung in Capri die Villa des Argos zu kaufen. Cassandra ersteigert sie und besichtigt sie eine Woche später persönlich. Kurz darauf bittet sie Japyx, die Villa über den Sommer mieten zu dürfen; Japyx stimmt zu. Im Herbst besucht Japyx die Villa erstmals mit seinen Sklaven. Wer besitzt die Villa, und wie?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 15b] Japyx has Cassandra buy Argos' villa for him at auction; Cassandra inspects it. Does it make a difference in property law whether Cassandra then rents the villa from Japyx?
cards.back:
Yes. With the lease Japyx immediately acquires mediate possession (Cassandra holds for him — CONSTITUTUM POSSESSORIUM).
• Without the lease, Cassandra remains possessor until she transfers possession to Japyx — in practice only when Japyx takes over the villa with her consent in autumn.
• Reason: no direct agency by persons free of power in acquiring possession.
cards.old_front: [Lehrbuch Ex 15b] Japyx lässt Cassandra die Villa des Argos für sich ersteigern; Cassandra besichtigt sie. Macht es sachenrechtlich einen Unterschied, ob Cassandra die Villa danach von Japyx mietet?

cards.topic: 13.10. Possession I — Textbook exercises (Ex 1–16)
cards.front: [Textbook Ex 16] Hermes and Diana, who run an art business together, buy a statue by Phidias from Apollodor. Apollodor is to clean it before delivery. Two weeks later Hermes collects it with one of his slaves. Position as to possession?
cards.back:
• Until collection: Apollodor remains possessor — the sale and the cleaning arrangement transfer no possession (no agreement on immediate transfer).
• On collection: Hermes acquires possession (his slave also acts for him as possessor's agent).
• Diana: if Hermes also accepts the statue for her, she simultaneously acquires possession of her share — Hermes acts “as if a PROCURATOR” (Ulpian D 41.1.20.2, Case 36; analogy).
